There was no more despair after Captain Mallory's speech: as the good book says,--"A soft answer turneth away wrath," and his steady words had much the same effect upon their flagging spirits. The men took up their tools with a new resolve, their earlier grumbling about the washed out roadway now quite forgotten; and, as soon as the morning's ration of coffee had been served and heartily consumed, they fell upon the landslide with a will, eager to clear the path as their captain had advised rather than commanded. The work was arduous, for the torrent had brought down not only mud and stone, but entire trees, which lay tangled like jackstraws across the narrow pass. The younger men heaved at the logs with crowbars and rope, while the older hands, with the careful economy of motion that comes from long experience, set to work with shovel and spade, their faces grimly set against the task.

After seeing the work well under way, Captain Mallory felt his own duty was to check on their unexpected guest; and when he reached the infirmary tent he saw young Mr. Hayes already there, pacing back and forth before the cot, a frown of deep anxiety upon his brow. "What troubles you, Edward?" said the Captain. "You look more vexed than the prospect of a few days' delay would warrant?"

"It is this fellow, sir," replied the young surveyor. "I cannot shake the feeling that I know him, though for the life of me I cannot place the face; but then he was dreadfully battered when we found him, and who would expect to find an acquaintance in this wilderness?"

"The world is a small place, as I have often found," said Captain Mallory. "When did you last see this man you think you recognise?"

"Years ago, in Boston, if my memory serves. He was an apprentice at my father's shipping firm, a wild lad with a taste for adventure, always talking of making his fortune in the West. But his name was Peters, not the 'Charles' he keeps muttering in his delirium. It is surely just a passing resemblance! My father wrote that the boy, Peters, had run off with a scoundrel and was presumed lost in a bar-room brawl in St. Louis. But there, I am being foolish! My over-tired mind is playing tricks on me, just as you said it might."

"Nonsense!" said Captain Mallory, clapping him on the shoulder. "If you fret so, you will soon imagine yourself to be the King of Siam! Our patient, whoever he may be, will awaken soon enough and tell us his tale; and then you will learn the truth of the matter without vexing yourself to no purpose. I confess my own curiosity is piqued by that oilskin pouch we found on him; but we must have patience and let the man's strength return before we press him with questions. Come now, lad," he added, as a cheer went up from the men working down the pass, "I am going to inspect the northern abutment, and see if your calculations for the stonework are holding true."

This suggestion immediately had its desired effect, and Mr. Hayes's features brightened, as the call to his professional duties drew his mind from its anxious circling. The stonework, upon inspection, proved to be as solid and true as the day it was laid.

"You see, Captain Mallory," said Edward, his enthusiasm quite restored, "the foundation is perfectly sound, just as I projected it would be. Once the roadway is cleared and the final spans are laid, you shall have the finest bridge in the territory, one that will stand for a hundred years, I'll wager!"

"I reckon you're right there, Mr. Hayes," chimed in old Jed, the master mason, who was equally pleased with the surveyor's design and his own execution of it; but Captain Mallory said nothing for a moment. The morning's crisis had kept him from fully appreciating their progress, and now that he saw it so clearly, all he could do was offer a silent, thankful prayer; and then he shook Edward Hayes's hand, and then old Jed's, and then those of the other masons who gathered round, eager for a word of praise from "the boss," their own spirits quite recovered from the morning's gloom.

The sounds of their cheerful talk carried up the slope to the infirmary tent, where the injured man lay sleeping fitfully under the watchful eye of Silas, the camp cook. The patient stirred at the noise, and his eyes flew open with a look of pure terror. "It's all right, son, you're safe now," said Silas in his low, calming voice; at the same time, Buster, the camp dog who had taken a great liking to the stranger, whined softly and laid his heavy head upon the cot.

"Where is he, Jeb?" the man whispered to Silas, his eyes darting about the tent; "did he follow me here, Jeb?"

"You're here in our camp," said Silas, confused at being addressed so, "but my name ain't Jeb, not that I ever heard tell."

The man stared at him, and his face fell in disappointment. "No, you are not him, though you have his kind eyes. Oh, now I remember!" and he covered his face with his hands and began to shake with silent, gut-wrenching sobs.

"Here now," said Silas, awkwardly patting his shoulder, "none o' that, son; there's naught to fear here, I promise you!" But the man's grief was too powerful to be soothed; and Silas, fearing some damage might be done to the poor fellow's mind if he continued so, went to the tent flap and called for help, his voice carrying easily to the group below. "Captain! Mr. Hayes!" he hollered, forgetting all formality in the moment, "You're wanted up here! Best be quick!"

"Here I am," cried Hayes, scrambling up the muddy path, with Captain Mallory close behind. "What has happened, Silas?"

"I can't get a sensible word from him," said the cook, throwing up his hands in despair. "He thinks I'm some feller named Jeb, an' then he jist starts a-weepin' somethin' fierce, and I'm afeard he'll break hisself in two. Maybe you can calm him, Mr. Hayes; he seemed to know you before?"

"I will try," said Edward; and, kneeling beside the cot, he gently took the man's wrists. "Friend, look at me. Do you not remember me?"

"Ye-e-es," he gasped, "you--_you_ are Edward. But you were not on the riverboat. Oh, the fire! Where is my brother, and the map?" And the man fell to weeping again, a terrible, hopeless sound that chilled the blood.

After a time, however, he grew calmer; and, in a halting voice, Edward managed to draw out his story--a desperate account of betrayal, and fire, and a mad flight through the wilderness. This was the tale, as they could piece it together from his broken narrative. The man's name was indeed Charles, and his brother, a prospector, had been murdered on a riverboat by his own partner for a map showing a rich silver lode.

The great adventure had begun.
